summary: Describes how to carry DTMF (touch-tone) signals, other tones and telephony events inside RTP packets. It lets key presses and tones cross an Internet voice call as data. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4733 and RFC 4734.

eli5.summary: When you press a number on a phone, it beeps a tone. This explains how to send a note that says which button was pressed, instead of the beep itself, over an Internet call.

questions: how to carry dtmf in voice calls
subtitle: A way to send touch tones and telephony signals inside Internet voice calls.

tldr.problem: Voice calls over the Internet use low-bit-rate codecs that distort or eliminate DTMF tones (the beeps you hear when pressing phone buttons). Applications need a way to send these tones and other telephony signals reliably across Internet calls.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2833 defines two RTP payload formats: one for named telephone events like DTMF digits and tones (which gateways convert to real sounds), and another for raw multi-frequency tones. Routers can carry both the encoded event and the audio representation together for reliability.
tldr.outcome: Internet phones can reliably exchange touch tones, fax tones, and other telephony signals with PSTN gateways and other endpoints. RFC 4733 and RFC 4734 provide updated specifications.

today: RFC 2833 is a Proposed Standard defining how to carry DTMF and telephony events in RTP packets. It was replaced by RFC 4733 and RFC 4734, which provide current specifications.

sections.title: DTMF Tones in Internet Calls
sections.content:
Dual-tone multifrequency (DTMF) signaling produces the beeps heard when pressing phone buttons. When Internet voice calls use compressed audio codecs like G.723.1 or G.729, these codecs distort or eliminate DTMF tones, making them unrecognizable at the far end.

RFC 2833 defines separate RTP payload formats for carrying DTMF digits and other telephone signals instead of relying on codec-distorted audio. This is especially important for gateways connecting Internet calls to the PSTN, interactive voice-response systems that need button recognition, and RTP trunks carrying circuit-switched calls over IP. Both named events (like DTMF) and raw tones can be sent, and they can be combined with audio for redundancy.
sections.eli5: Internet voice codecs are designed for talking, not for beeping tones. So instead of trying to send the beep sound, we send a message saying 'the user pressed button 5', and the far end generates the beep or recognizes the button.

sections.title: Events versus Tones
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes between two approaches to handling DTMF and telephony signals. In the tone representation, a gateway measures the frequency components of voice-band signals and transmits the information without trying to understand what the tones mean. In the event representation, a gateway recognizes the tones and translates them into event names like 'DTMF 5' or 'ringing tone'.

Gateways may send both representations simultaneously using the redundancy mechanism defined in the RFC, allowing receivers to choose which form to use. If a gateway cannot generate tone waveforms, it should send both the named event payload and regular audio encoding to allow the receiver to render tones. The choice between events and tones affects whether the receiver recognizes the meaning of signals (events) or simply regenerates the waveforms (tones).
sections.eli5: One way is to send a note saying 'play a 5 on the phone', which means 'the user pressed 5'. Another way is to send the exact sound wave. Different receivers prefer different methods.

sections.title: Named Telephone Event Payload
sections.content:
The payload format for named telephone events uses a 4-byte header containing the event code (0-255), an end-of-event bit, a reserved bit, a volume field (for DTMF), and a duration field. The duration, in timestamp units, indicates how long the event has lasted; for an 8 kHz sampling rate, this can represent events up to about 8 seconds.

Senders transmit event packets as soon as they recognize an event and continue every 50 milliseconds or at the audio codec's packet interval. If the event continues, the sender retransmits with an updated duration. To ensure receivers get complete information even if the final packet is lost, senders transmit the event at least three times or until the next event appears. The end bit indicates when the event has completed.
sections.eli5: Each message is a small label that says what happened, how loud it was, and how long it lasted. We keep sending updates as long as the event is happening, like a running counter.

sections.title: Telephone Event Types
sections.content:
RFC 2833 defines five categories of telephone events: DTMF tones (0-9, *, #, A-D), fax and modem tones (such as ANS, CNG, V.21), standard subscriber line tones (dial tone, ringing, busy), country-specific tones (comfort tone, special information), and trunk signaling events. Compliant implementations must support DTMF digits and most subscriber line tones, though specific subsets can be disabled through configuration.

For example, DTMF digit '5' is encoded as event 5, the asterisk as 10, and the hash as 11. Fax tones include the Answer Tone (ANS) used to disable echo suppression, and V.21 signaling used for Group 3 fax. Line events include dial tone (indicating the exchange is ready), ringing tone (call alerting), and busy tone. The RFC defines 90+ event codes and their meanings so that gateways and endpoints can interoperate.
sections.eli5: There are different kinds of beeps: button presses, fax sounds, and phone line tones. Each one gets its own number code in the message.

sections.title: Handling Packet Loss
sections.content:
The RFC uses the redundancy mechanism from RFC 2198, which allows multiple past events to be included in a single packet. This provides error resiliency: if a packet containing an event is lost, the redundant copy in the next packet can still be received. The timestamp offset in the redundancy header has 14 bits, allowing a single packet to represent events spanning up to 2.048 seconds at 8 kHz sampling.

Alternatively, an encoder can treat the event payload as a highly-compressed version of the audio frame, including both the event code and the audio codec rendition in the same packet. This allows endpoints that don't understand the event format to still function, since they can fall back to the audio codec. However, since event payloads (4 bytes) are much smaller than audio frames, the redundancy approach is more efficient for reliable transmission.
sections.eli5: If a message gets lost, we send the information again in the next packet. Or we can include the sound itself in the packet too, so even if the message is lost, the receiver can still hear the beep.

sections.title: Deployment and Interoperability
sections.content:
Receivers can advertise which events they support using the Session Description Protocol (SDP) with the 'fmtp' parameter. For example, an endpoint can declare it handles DTMF 0-15, dial tone (66), and ringing tone (70). Since all compliant implementations must handle DTMF 0-15, listing these is optional.

The RFC also addresses timing: the default timestamp rate is 8 kHz, though other rates may be defined. Sources and receivers must be prepared to handle overlap between tone events and regular audio, which is likely at tone onset and necessary to avoid interpretation errors. When rendering tones at a gateway, implementations should use the encoded event rather than audio-rendered tones, since compressed codecs may introduce spurious artifacts.
sections.eli5: Receivers can tell senders which beeps they understand, and both sides need to be ready if the beep message and the audio arrive at slightly different times.

fields.name: Event Code
fields.desc: The event type (0-9 for DTMF, 10 for *, 11 for #, 32+ for tones)

fields.name: E (End)
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the event ends

fields.name: R (Reserved)
fields.desc: Reserved for future use, must be 0

fields.name: Volume
fields.desc: Power level in dBm0 for DTMF (0 to -63 dBm0)

fields.name: Duration
fields.desc: How long the event has lasted in timestamp units
